title: The UGC Creator Programme
description: Hooks that stop a scroll. Scripts that sell without sounding like an ad. Footage that looks like real life, not a studio. Edits people actually finish watching. And a pitch that gets you paid for it. That's the whole path: 32 lessons, and every single one leaves you with something built, filmed, or sent, not just watched.

modules.title: The UGC Creator Blueprint
modules.frame: Before you film a single second, you need to know what you're actually being paid for, and it isn't “holding a phone and talking.” This module sets the bar, gets your setup production-ready, and installs the habits every module after this one leans on.

lessons.title: What Actually Separates a Pro From an Amateur in UGC
lessons.overview: Here's the lesson that saves you a year of guessing: UGC isn't “hold phone, talk to camera.” It's a performance job. Brands don't rehire you because they liked you. They rehire you because your numbers did something. This lesson breaks down exactly what separates a one-off gig from a real retainer: reliability, brand-safety instincts, and shooting for the edit instead of just filming.
lessons.interactive: Watch 3 real ad examples below. Give each one a score from 1 to 10 on three things, then compare your scores to ours.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your 3 scores (Brief Fit, Hookiness, Editability for each ad) and 2–3 sentences on which one you scored most differently from ClickClick's team, and why.

activity.prompt: For each ad, score it 1–10 on Brief Fit, Hookiness, and Editability (see what each one means next to the boxes). Then tap Compare to see how ClickClick's team scored it.

criteria.label: Brief Fit
criteria.hint: Did it do what the brand actually asked for?

criteria.label: Hookiness
criteria.hint: Does it grab you in the first second?

criteria.label: Editability
criteria.hint: Does it give an editor good clips to cut to?

subjects.label: Example 1: a cast-iron cookware ad for a cooking-niche client (real UGC, by @maddyoutdoors.coach)
subjects.note: The product is held up and named almost immediately, and the on-screen text does the job a verbal hook usually does. Solid Brief Fit and Editability; there's room to make the opening moment itself more of a scroll-stopper.

subjects.label: Example 2: a tumbler/drinkware ad for an outdoor-niche client (real UGC, by @maddyoutdoors.coach)
subjects.note: The close-up pour shot gives an editor something to cut to straight away, and the branding is clearly visible without feeling like a product shot. A clean, native-feeling example of shooting for the edit.

subjects.label: Example 3: a prenatal vitamin ad for Naternal Vitamins (real UGC, by @ugcwithmaddyt)
subjects.note: No on-screen text doing the work here, just two real people sharing a genuine-feeling moment with the product. That's harder to pull off than it looks, which is why it scores highest on Hookiness: it doesn't read as an ad at all.

lessons.title: The Creator Workflow: Brief to Delivery
lessons.overview: Every missed deadline and every awkward client email traces back to the same broken step. This lesson walks the full pipeline a working creator runs on every paid job: brief, script, shot list, filming day, footage triage, delivery, and shows you exactly where it usually breaks. (Spoiler: it's almost always the shot list.)
lessons.interactive: Take an 8-step production checklist and put it in the order you'd actually run it on a real job.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your completed checklist sequence and your own one-page "Creator SOP": the exact steps you commit to running on every job.

activity.prompt: Put this 8-step production checklist into the order a working creator actually runs it.
items: Read the brief twice, once for the ask and once for what's implied but not written
Confirm usage rights, deadline and revision count in writing
Draft the script
Get script sign-off from the client
Build the shot list
Film
Triage footage: select the best takes
Edit and deliver in the agreed format

lessons.title: Building the Ultimate Home Studio, on Any Budget
lessons.overview: You don't need a studio to shoot like a pro, but the wrong gear will quietly cap everything you make. This lesson covers three real tiers, Starter (£150 / $190), Working Pro (£600 / $760), Studio (£2,000+ / $2,500+), across lighting, audio, mounting, and background, and tells you straight which upgrade actually moves the needle for your kind of content.

lessons.deliverable: Submit your gear-allocation sheet plus a photo of your current setup, marked up with what you'd change first and why.

lessons.title: Your Creator Operating System
lessons.overview: This is the boring lesson that quietly decides whether you last a year in this or burn out by month three. Calendar, deal tracker, invoice template, file-naming convention: the unglamorous system that lets you scale instead of re-inventing your process on every single job.
lessons.interactive: Take the deal-tracker and footage-naming templates and adapt them to your own niche and file structure.
lessons.deliverable: Upload a screenshot of your customised deal tracker with at least 2 entries, and your finalised file-naming convention written out in full.

modules.title: Reverse-Engineering Winning Hooks
modules.frame: You've got about one second before a thumb decides your video isn't worth its time. This module is entirely about winning that second, on command, for any product, not just the ones you feel inspired about.

lessons.title: The Psychology of the First 3 Seconds
lessons.overview: A thumb decides to stop scrolling before your brain even finishes the sentence you're saying. This lesson is the psychology behind that decision: four levers (curiosity gap, pattern interrupt, stakes, relatability) that force a thumb to stop moving, on command.
lessons.interactive: See two openings back to back, predict which one would stop the scroll, then see the reasoning behind the answer.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your 5 predictions with accuracy score, and a written breakdown of the lever the top-performing hook used.

activity.prompt: Which opening actually stopped the scroll? Pick one, then see why.

questions.q: Opener A: “Hi guys, so today I wanted to show you…”  vs  Opener B: “I got fired for doing this on camera.”
questions.explain: B wins. It's a curiosity gap plus stakes in one line. A is the single most common mistake in this course: burning the first second on a greeting.

questions.q: Opener A: a slow zoom on a product box, no voice yet  vs  Opener B: the creator mid-sentence, already reacting to something off-camera
questions.explain: B, pattern interrupt. It looks like you scrolled into the middle of something already happening, which reads as more real than a staged product shot.

questions.q: Opener A: “3 things nobody tells you about [product]”  vs  Opener B: “This product is really good, here's why”
questions.explain: A, the specific number plus “nobody tells you” is a concrete curiosity gap. B is a bold claim with nothing pulling the viewer forward.

lessons.title: Hook Autopsy: 20 Viral Hooks, Broken Down
lessons.overview: Twenty hooks that actually worked, cut open and laid out flat. This is a structured teardown across beauty, tech, food, and fitness, sorted into the 6 archetypes that cover almost everything that scroll-stops: Problem-Agitate, Bold Claim, Relatable POV, Visual Pattern-Interrupt, Story Cold-Open, Direct Callout. Once you see the pattern, you can't unsee it.
lessons.interactive: Tag each hook line against the 6-archetype key, then check your answers with the reasoning behind each one.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your completed tagging sheet with your accuracy score, plus 3 hooks you'd personally steal-and-adapt for a ClickClick client.

activity.prompt: Tag each hook line to its archetype.

items.label: “If your skin does this in the shower, stop scrolling.”
“Nobody warns you how bad hotel pillows actually are.”
“This is the only product that's ever actually worked for my hair.”
“POV: you just found out your ex is dating your dentist.”
[Camera whip-pans to a messy desk] “Okay so THIS is what I've been hiding.”
“So it's 2am and I get this text from my landlord…”

lessons.title: The Pattern-Interrupt Scripting Framework
lessons.overview: Staring at a blank page is where most hooks die. This lesson kills that problem for good with a repeatable 4-line formula: Interrupt → Stakes → Promise → Proof-Tease, plus a bank of 30 fill-in-the-blank openers sorted by niche, so you're never starting from nothing again.
lessons.interactive: Plug a real product (yours or a given one) into the 4-line formula and build your own hook, then compare it against a worked example.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your 3 hook variants written out in full, each line labeled with the formula slot it fills.

activity.prompt: Plug a reusable water bottle into the 4-line formula.

fields.label: Interrupt
fields.model: “I've bought six water bottles this year. This is the last one.”

fields.label: Stakes
fields.placeholder: what's at risk if they don't act
fields.model: “Because the other five all did the same thing: cracked, leaked, or started smelling like a gym bag after a month.”

fields.label: Promise
fields.model: “This one's actually leak-proof, I've thrown it in my bag upside down for three months straight.”

fields.label: Proof-Tease
fields.placeholder: a hint of evidence to come
fields.model: “Watch what happens when I shake it over my white couch.”

lessons.title: Hook Writing Sprint & Peer Review
lessons.overview: Twelve minutes. Eight hooks. One product you didn't pick. This lesson puts you under the same pressure a real job does, then hands your work to peer review: the fastest, cheapest way to find out your instincts are off before a client's actual budget finds out for you.
lessons.interactive: Run your own 8 sprint hooks through this checklist before you post any of them.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your 8 sprint hooks, your 3 completed peer reviews, and your self-selected top 2 to carry into Module 3.

activity.prompt: Before you post any of your 8 sprint hooks, run each one through this check.

items.text: Under 3 seconds spoken out loud
Uses one of the 4 levers: curiosity gap, pattern interrupt, stakes, or relatability
Doesn't open with a greeting (“Hey guys”, “So today…”)
You'd personally stop scrolling for it, honestly

modules.title: Advanced Direct-Response Scriptwriting
modules.frame: A great hook that leads nowhere is just a great trailer for nothing. This module builds the 30–45 seconds after the hook: the part that actually turns a watch into a sale.

lessons.title: Direct-Response Fundamentals for Short-Form
lessons.overview: Stop writing movie scripts. A UGC script is a direct-response sales letter that's been shrunk down to 30 seconds, and it has a structure whether you've noticed it or not. This lesson maps Hook → Agitate → Bridge → Offer → CTA onto real short-form pacing so you can build one on purpose instead of by accident.
lessons.interactive: Label each line of a real script to its role in the Hook, Agitate, Bridge, Offer, CTA structure.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your 5 annotated scripts, plus one line naming the structural mistake you catch most often in your own past work.

activity.prompt: Label each line of this script to its role in the Hook → Agitate → Bridge → Offer → CTA structure.

items.label: “I used to iron my sheets every single week.”
“Which, if you've ever done it, you know eats your entire Sunday.”
“Then I found a fabric spray that drops the wrinkles out in the dryer.”
“It's £14 / $18, one bottle lasts about 4 months.”
“Link's in my bio if your Sundays are as ruined as mine were.”

lessons.title: Value Propositions & Benefit Stacking
lessons.overview: “12-hour battery” is a spec. “Never dies mid-shift” is a reason to buy. This lesson lives in that gap, and shows you how to stack three real benefits inside 10 seconds without the script starting to sound like you're reading off the box.
lessons.interactive: Translate raw product features into benefit lines, against the clock.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your 10 translated lines and your strongest 3-benefit stack, submitted as a ready-to-read script excerpt.

activity.prompt: Translate each raw feature into a benefit line.

fields.label: “12-hour battery”
fields.model: “Charge it Sunday night, forget about it till Friday.”

fields.label: “Recycled aluminium body”
fields.model: “Drop-tested: mine's survived two flights of stairs and a dog.”

fields.label: “Compatible with any charger”
fields.model: “No new cable to lose, no drawer full of the wrong one.”

lessons.title: Writing CTAs That Actually Convert
lessons.overview: “Link in bio” is the single most wasted line in short-form video: it's your last chance to move someone, spent on nothing. This lesson gives you 5 real CTA types (Urgency, Social-Proof-Close, Risk-Reversal, Curiosity-Loop, Direct-Command) and exactly which funnel stage each one is built to close.
lessons.interactive: Match each CTA type to the funnel stage it's actually built to close.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your 5 CTA variants labeled by type, with your own pick marked and one sentence on why it fits.

activity.prompt: Pick the CTA type built for each funnel stage.

questions.q: A viewer who's never heard of the brand before, still deciding if this is even relevant to them
questions.explain: Curiosity-Loop. At this stage they're not ready to buy, they're ready to keep watching or tap through. Urgency and hard commands feel pushy this early.

questions.q: A viewer who's watched the whole video and is visibly nodding along
questions.explain: Direct-Command. They're sold, so tell them exactly what to do next. Don't add friction with more convincing.

questions.q: A viewer who's interested but has been burned by a bad purchase before
questions.explain: Risk-Reversal. A return policy or guarantee removes the exact objection they're sitting on.

lessons.title: Full Script Assembly: Hook to CTA
lessons.overview: Everything from the last two modules comes together here: one complete, production-ready 30–45 second script, for a real or assigned product, timed against a stopwatch instead of a word count. This is the script you'll actually shoot.
lessons.interactive: Read your script out loud against a stopwatch, so you catch pacing issues text alone hides.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your final written script plus a voice-memo table-read, timed and under the 45-second cap.

activity.prompt: Read your script out loud against a stopwatch and check each marker.

items.text: Hook lands by 0:03
First specific benefit stated by 0:08
CTA starts with at least 5 seconds left on the clock
Full read, start to finish, is under 0:45

modules.title: High-Converting Production & Real-Life B-Roll Masterclass
modules.frame: This is where it stops being theory and starts being a camera in your hand. Lighting, framing, and the one skill that separates paid creators from hobbyists: making a product look like it belongs in someone's actual life, not staged on a white table.

lessons.title: Lighting on a Budget
lessons.overview: A great script filmed under bad light still looks like it was shot for free. This lesson adapts 3-point lighting for a bedroom or kitchen (one window, one cheap LED panel, one bounce card) and names the 4 lighting mistakes that quietly make even strong work look unpaid.
lessons.interactive: Diagnose the specific fix (angle, colour temp, diffusion, position) for four common lighting problems.
lessons.deliverable: Film and upload a 10-second test clip using only natural light plus one bounce card, applying the fix from your weakest diagnosis.

activity.prompt: Diagnose the fix for each lighting problem.

questions.q: Footage looks orange/yellow under a warm bulb
questions.explain: Colour temp. Mixing a warm bulb with daylight causes the orange cast, so match the light source or correct white balance.

questions.q: Face is lit but has a hard, unflattering shadow down one side
options: Add diffusion (a cheap shower curtain works)
questions.explain: Diffusion softens a hard shadow far more effectively than distance or dimming. It spreads the light source instead of shrinking it.

questions.q: Subject is lit but blends into an equally-bright background
options: Add separation: dim or move the background light
questions.explain: Without separation between subject and background brightness, the shot reads flat regardless of angle.

questions.q: Light is coming from directly overhead, casting shadows under the eyes
options: Lower or angle the light closer to eye-level
questions.explain: Overhead light is the single most common “why does this look unpaid” cause. Dropping the angle closer to eye-level fixes it instantly.

lessons.title: Framing, Angles & Camera Movement
lessons.overview: Six shot types cover almost every UGC video you'll ever film: talking-head medium, close-up reaction, POV hand-shot, over-shoulder demo, static product hero, walk-and-talk. Learn them on command and you'll never stand in a room wondering what to film next.
lessons.interactive: Assign the correct shot type to every line of a rough script.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your shot-annotated script, then film and upload one example each of your 2 weakest shot types.

activity.prompt: Assign the right shot type to each script line.

items.label: “So here's what happened when I tried it…” (delivering to camera)
The moment right after tasting/using it, no words, just the face
Unscrewing the cap and pouring it out
Showing a friend how to use it, camera behind your shoulder
The product sitting on a shelf, camera slowly settles on it
Explaining the product while walking through your kitchen

lessons.title: Capturing Aesthetic, Real-Life Product B-Roll
lessons.overview: This is the skill the whole course is really built around. Not filming a product, making it look like it already belongs in someone's real, lived-in life instead of staged on a white table. Composition, prop-styling with stuff you already own, and the 3-angle-minimum rule for every beat of b-roll.
lessons.interactive: Build a 6-shot b-roll list before you film, covering at least 3 different angle types.
lessons.deliverable: Film and upload your full 6-shot b-roll sequence of a real product in a real, lived-in setting: kitchen, desk, bathroom counter, car. No white background.

activity.prompt: Build a 6-shot b-roll list from this menu. Pick at least 6, and don't just repeat the same angle.

items.text: Wide shot: product on the counter, whole scene in frame
Medium shot: hands entering frame to pick it up
Close-up: label / texture / detail
Wide shot: product in use in the background of a normal activity
Medium shot: product being opened or poured
Close-up: the reaction moment, in-hand
Overhead: product laid out with 2–3 other items
Close-up: product being put back down / put away
Medium shot: product next to something that shows scale
Wide shot: the empty scene, product about to enter frame

lessons.title: The Multi-Shot Product Story
lessons.overview: Individual shots are just footage. Sequenced right (context → interaction → payoff) they become a story that carries the script instead of just filling dead air. This is the exact skill that turns “footage” into “a cut.”
lessons.interactive: Arrange 8 b-roll shots into the strongest context, interaction, payoff order.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your own filmed sequence, built from your 4.03 footage, edited into a 15–20 second silent story cut.

activity.prompt: Arrange these 8 b-roll shots into the strongest context → interaction → payoff order.
items: Wide: the room/setting, product not yet visible
Medium: product enters frame, placed on the surface
Close-up: label or packaging detail
Medium: hand reaches in and picks it up
POV: using it
Close-up: the moment it takes effect / the reaction
Medium: result visible, the payoff
Wide: back to the room, now changed by the payoff

modules.title: Retention Editing in CapCut
modules.frame: Raw footage is not a video. It's raw material. This module is the edit: pacing, captions, and sound, treated like the data problem it actually is, not something you eyeball and hope for.

lessons.title: Timeline Pacing & the Retention Curve
lessons.overview: A retention graph doesn't lie. It shows you the exact second someone got bored and left. This lesson teaches you to read one and reverse-engineer the edit decisions, cut length, and moment placement that caused every drop.
lessons.interactive: Match 4 retention curves to the edit style that caused each one.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your 4 matches with reasoning, plus one edited 5-second segment from your own footage cut to under 2-second average shot length.

activity.prompt: Match each retention curve to the edit style that caused it.
categories: Holds high, small drop only at the CTA

items.label: Edit A: 8-second static product shot before any hook
Edit B: 2-second average shot length throughout, no single weak point
Edit C: strong hook, but every cut after is the same length and pacing never varies
Edit D: strong first half, then a 6-second unbroken talking segment appears

lessons.title: Jump Cuts & Visual Rhythm in CapCut
lessons.overview: This is hands-on, inside CapCut: clean jump-cut execution, J/L-cut audio bridging, and building a rhythm so your cuts feel intentional, not like you just chopped out the boring bits and hoped nobody noticed.
lessons.interactive: Confirm each step of your own jump-cut build in CapCut against a short checklist.
lessons.deliverable: Export and upload your own 15-second jump-cut edit, built from your Module 4 footage.

activity.prompt: Confirm each step of your jump-cut build in CapCut.

items.text: Cut on action, not on silence
No jump cut sits longer than 2 seconds
At least one J-cut or L-cut audio bridge used
Exported and previewed at full speed, not just scrubbed

lessons.title: Dynamic Captioning That Holds Attention
lessons.overview: Static bottom-third captions are basically wallpaper. Nobody's attention holds on them. This lesson covers keyword emphasis, caption timing matched to speech rhythm, and how to clean up CapCut's auto-captions to broadcast quality, fast.
lessons.interactive: Match the right caption treatment to the scenario it's built for.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your final captioned edit with keyword emphasis applied to at least 5 words across the clip.

activity.prompt: Which caption treatment holds attention in each scenario?

questions.q: A fast, punchy hook line with one word that matters most
options: Word-by-word reveal with the key word scaled up
questions.explain: Keyword emphasis timed to the beat is what makes captions add energy instead of just transcribing.

questions.q: A longer explainer sentence in the middle of the video
options: One giant caption for the whole sentence
Short phrase chunks, timed to speech rhythm
Captions that appear all at once, ahead of the audio
questions.explain: Chunking to speech rhythm keeps captions readable without viewers finishing the line before you say it, which kills suspense.

lessons.title: Sound Design for Scroll-Stopping Content
lessons.overview: Sound is the last 10% nobody notices until it's missing. This lesson layers trending audio, SFX whooshes and impacts right on the cut points, and a basic voice-EQ pass: the difference between an edit that feels professional and one that just feels homemade.
lessons.interactive: Confirm your own sound design pass against a short checklist.
lessons.deliverable: Export and upload your fully sound-designed final edit: Module 4 b-roll, Module 3 script, and Module 5 editing, complete.

activity.prompt: Confirm your sound design pass.

items.text: One music bed added, ducked under speech
At least 3 SFX hits landed exactly on cut points
Voice EQ / cleanup applied

modules.title: The Business, Pitching & Brand Deal Playbook
modules.frame: None of the last five modules pay you until this one. Portfolio, outreach, pricing, and the contract clause that's the difference between an invoice that gets paid and one that gets ignored.

lessons.title: Building a Portfolio That Sells
lessons.overview: A brand decides whether to keep watching your reel in about 8 seconds, and most creators waste that window leading with their most recent clip instead of their strongest one. This lesson fixes that: what brands actually screen for, and how to structure a 5-video reel that leads with your best work, on purpose.
lessons.interactive: Pick and order your strongest 5-clip reel from 8 clips, the first 3 positions matter most.
lessons.deliverable: Upload your own 5-video portfolio reel, built entirely from work completed across this course.

activity.prompt: You have 8 clips. Pick and order your strongest 5-clip reel. Only the first 5 positions are checked, and order matters most for the first 3.
items: Your single best result: most views, most obviously “worked”
Your most technically polished edit
A clip for a recognizable or premium brand, if you have one
A clip that shows range: different niche or format than the rest
A clip with strong on-camera delivery, even if the product is minor
A decent but unremarkable clip
Your oldest / weakest clip
A clip that's technically fine but has no clear hook

lessons.title: Cold Outreach That Gets Replies
lessons.overview: Most cold pitches die unread. This lesson is the anatomy of the ones that don't: subject line, a first-line hook (yes, the same skill from Module 2, it works on brands too), research specific enough to prove you're not mass-emailing, and an ask with almost no friction.
lessons.interactive: Rewrite a weak cold-pitch opener using the framework, then compare it against a model rewrite.
lessons.deliverable: Submit one real cold pitch email, written for an actual brand you'd like to work with, ready to send.

activity.prompt: Rewrite this weak cold pitch opener.

fields.label: Weak: “Hi, I love your brand and would love to work with you! Let me know your rates.”
fields.model: “Hey [Name], noticed [Brand]'s last 3 reels all used voiceover instead of on-camera talent. I make UGC that performs like [specific result]. Happy to send 2 sample clips built around your actual product if useful?”

lessons.title: Pricing Your Work & Packaging Offers
lessons.overview: “What should I charge?” is the question that keeps creators broke for way longer than it should. This lesson replaces the guesswork with a real rate framework (usage rights, exclusivity, volume) and 3 ready-to-use package tiers: single-video, bundle, retainer, worked in both £ and $ so it travels with you.
lessons.interactive: Plug your experience level and a sample brief into the calculator to generate a defensible quote in £ or $.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your calculated rate card across all 3 package tiers, in your own currency, with your reasoning for each price.

activity.prompt: Calculate a defensible quote for a sample brief: 1 video, paid social usage.
activity.modelNote: This is a floor, not a ceiling. Exclusivity, whitelisting/ad-spend rights, and rush turnarounds all add on top.

lessons.title: Contracts, Usage Rights & Getting Paid
lessons.overview: This is the lesson that actually gets you paid, or saves you from a client who was never going to pay you anyway. The 5 non-negotiable clauses every UGC contract needs: usage term, usage scope, revision limit, payment terms, kill fee, and the red flags that mean you walk, no matter how good the brand name looks.
lessons.interactive: Review a sample contract's clause list and flag every one that's missing or unfavorable.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your annotated red-flag list, plus your own filled-in contract template, ready to send to your next client: the course's final deliverable.

activity.prompt: Review this sample contract's clause list and flag every one that's missing or unfavorable.

items.text: Usage term is stated anywhere in the contract (this one doesn't say how long they can use it)
Usage scope says: “paid and organic, all platforms, worldwide, in perpetuity”
Revision limit is capped at 2 rounds
Payment terms: “Net 60, upon client's discretion”
There is no kill fee clause anywhere in the contract

modules.title: Beyond the Client Job
modules.frame: Client work pays the bills, but it's not the whole game. This module covers the parts that don't show up in a brief: reading your own numbers, getting paid for how a video actually gets used, selling live instead of just posting, and building an audience of your own so brands start coming to you instead of the other way around.

lessons.title: Reading Your Numbers Like a Pro
lessons.overview: A view is not a result. This lesson breaks down what your numbers are actually telling you: reach metrics that show how far something travelled, resonance metrics that show whether anyone cared, and conversion metrics that show whether it made anyone act, so you stop chasing the wrong one.
lessons.interactive: Match five real post scenarios to the metric category that actually judges them: reach, resonance, or conversion.
lessons.deliverable: Submit a real post of yours (any platform) with its view count, comment/save/share count, and one sentence on which metric mattered most for what that post was actually trying to do.

activity.prompt: Match each scenario to the metric category that actually judges it.

items.label: Total view count on a brand-awareness campaign
Follower growth after a video goes semi-viral
Comments and saves on a video that resonated
Shares from people tagging friends
Link-clicks and purchases from a direct-response ad

lessons.title: Getting Paid What You're Owed
lessons.overview: Two creators can shoot the identical video and get paid completely different amounts, because usage is priced separately from the shoot. This lesson breaks down what usage scope, whitelisting, and exclusivity actually mean, so you stop pricing a video like it's only ever going on the brand's own page.
lessons.interactive: Review a usage-rights request and flag every line that's missing or unfavorable, same skill as the contract check, aimed specifically at usage.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your annotated flag list, plus one sentence on what you'd ask the brand to add or change before signing.

activity.prompt: Review this usage-rights request and flag every line that's missing or unfavorable.

items.text: Usage scope explicitly says “organic only”, with paid usage listed as a separate, additional fee
The brief says “usage: everywhere, forever” with no separate paid-usage line
Exclusivity (you can't work with competitor brands) is mentioned with no time limit
Whitelisting access is requested with no mention of ad spend duration or platform
The paid-usage fee is stated as a flat add-on, separate from the shoot fee

lessons.title: Selling Live Without Freezing Up
lessons.overview: A static video pitches once and moves on. A live stream has to keep re-selling the same product to new people joining every few seconds, which means the structure has to loop instead of run in a straight line. This lesson breaks down the segment order that keeps a live selling stream working the whole way through.
lessons.interactive: Put this live-selling segment loop into the order that actually keeps a stream working.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your own live-selling segment outline for a real or assumed product, following this loop structure, timed to roughly how long you'd run each segment.

activity.prompt: Arrange this live-selling loop into the order that keeps a stream working.
items: Welcome new viewers and restate what's being sold, for anyone who just joined
Show the product in use, not just held up to camera
State the price and the deal clearly, out loud
Create urgency, a countdown, limited stock, or a time-boxed discount
Answer 1-2 real comments on screen, by name
Loop back to the welcome and restate the offer again

lessons.title: Building Your Own Audience While You Work for Others
lessons.overview: Brands don't just hire talent, they hire proof. A creator who posts consistently under their own name is showing exactly what a client would get, before the client ever has to risk a booking on them. This lesson is about building that proof: picking a small number of recurring topics, called content pillars, so your own feed reads as something instead of random.
lessons.interactive: Answer a few quick questions on what actually makes a content pillar work.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your own 2-3 content pillars, plus one real post idea for each.

activity.prompt: Quick check: what actually makes a content pillar work?

questions.q: Which is a real content pillar, not just a random post?
options: A recurring “products that actually work” series you post weekly
A trending sound you jumped on once
questions.explain: A pillar is something an audience can expect again. A one-off post, even a good one, doesn't build that expectation.

questions.q: Why do content pillars matter more than posting frequency alone?
options: They don't, frequency is all that matters
They give your feed a reason to be followed, not just watched once
They're required by every platform's algorithm
questions.explain: Frequency without a throughline just produces more random content. Pillars are what turn a viewer into a follower, because they know what they'll get next time.

questions.q: How many content pillars does the lesson recommend starting with?
questions.explain: 2-3 is enough to feel consistent without boxing you in. Too many and nothing reads as a pattern; just one gets stale fast.

modules.title: Barter, Gifting & Product Deals
modules.frame: Not every brand you want to work with has a marketing budget, and that doesn't make them not worth working with. This module is about the deals that involve product, not payment: when they're actually worth your time, how to pitch one that gets a yes, what to get in writing even when no money changes hands, and how to turn free-product work into your next paid booking instead of your last one.

lessons.title: When a Barter Deal Is Actually Worth It
lessons.overview: Internet advice loves to say working for free product is an insult. On the ground, it's more complicated than that. A local coffee roaster or a small skincare line often genuinely can't afford agency rates, but they do have real stock with a real RRP, and if it's something you'd buy anyway, a fair trade removes a real expense and builds your portfolio before any cash is on the table. The skill isn't refusing every gifting offer on principle. It's telling a good one apart from a bad one fast.
lessons.interactive: Decide whether you'd take 3 real-style gifting offers, then see the reasoning behind each call.
lessons.deliverable: Pick one gifting offer you could realistically get this month (real or made up), and write 2–3 sentences on whether you'd take it and why, using the same reasoning.

activity.prompt: Take it, or pass? Decide first, then see how ClickClick's team would call it.

questions.q: A local matcha café offers you a monthly product supply worth about £120 in exchange for 3 short organic videos a month. You already go there twice a week.
questions.explain: Take it. Real value close to what you'd already spend, for a product you genuinely use, from a brand that almost certainly can't afford your cash rate anyway. This is what a good barter deal looks like.

questions.q: A large fashion retailer with a national ad budget offers you one £15 t-shirt in exchange for 5 videos, full usage rights, and first refusal on your other brand deals for 6 months.
questions.explain: Pass. Low product value against a high ask, and a brand this size can clearly afford to pay cash. An exclusivity clause like “first refusal” belongs in a paid contract, not a free t-shirt.

questions.q: A new skincare brand with no reviews yet offers a full product bundle (RRP around £90) for one video, with no rights beyond reposting it on their own page.
questions.explain: Take it. Solid product value, one clear deliverable, no rights grab. Exactly the kind of low-risk trade worth doing early on, while you're still building proof of what you can shoot.

lessons.title: Pitching a Barter Deal Like a Pro
lessons.overview: Most gifting pitches get ignored, and it's rarely because the brand hates free content. It's because the message gave them nothing to say yes to: no proof, no specifics, no reason to trust a stranger with their stock. A good barter pitch reads like a real, low-effort trade between two people who already like the same thing, not a cold ask for a handout.
lessons.interactive: Two creators DM the same small brand asking for a barter deal. Only one gets a reply. Read both, then answer.
lessons.deliverable: Write your own 3–4 sentence barter pitch to a real (or imagined) small brand you'd actually want product from. Include proof you're a genuine fan, the exact trade you're offering, and how often.

activity.prompt: Read both pitches to the same small brand, then answer.

questions.q:
Pitch A: “Hiii I love your brand, could I get some free stuff to post about? I have a big following lol.”
Pitch B: “Hi! I'm in most weeks and already order your oat matcha 2–3x a week, here's a video I shot there last month: [link]. I'd love to trade 3 short organic videos a month for a standing product supply, happy to keep it casual, just let me know if that's useful for you.”
Which pitch actually gets a reply?
questions.explain: Pitch B. It proves they're already a real customer, links actual proof they can shoot content, states an exact trade, and makes it a low-effort yes. Pitch A asks for something with zero proof and a vague, self-focused reason.

questions.q: What's the one thing missing from Pitch A that makes it easy to reject?
options: Any proof they can actually shoot good content
questions.explain: Proof. Brands doing barter deals still want to see you can produce something worth trading for: a portfolio link, a past example, or at least a real reason you're already a customer.

questions.q: Which detail in Pitch B makes it easy for the brand to say yes fast?
options: It names an exact number of videos on an exact cadence, not a vague “let's collab”
questions.explain: The specifics. “3 videos a month” is a decision a busy small-brand owner can say yes to in ten seconds. “Let's collab sometime” is a decision they have to think about, so it usually gets ignored.

dmMockup.bad: Hiii I love your brand, could I get some free stuff to post about? I have a big following lol.
dmMockup.good: Hi! I'm in most weeks and already order your oat matcha 2–3x a week, here's a video I shot there last month: [link]. I'd love to trade 3 short organic videos a month for a standing product supply, happy to keep it casual, just let me know if that's useful for you.

lessons.title: What to Get in Writing, Even for Free Product
lessons.overview: No money changing hands doesn't mean nothing needs agreeing. A barter deal still needs a real scope (how many, how often, for how long), and in the UK and US you're still legally required to disclose gifted product, #ad or #gifted, on every post, no exceptions. A one-paragraph agreement before you film protects you from the most common barter problem: a brand quietly expecting more than what you agreed to.
lessons.interactive: Fill in the 4 lines of a lightweight barter agreement using your own real or planned deal.
lessons.deliverable: Submit your filled-in 4-line barter agreement, ready to send before your next trade.

activity.prompt: Fill in these 4 lines before you say yes to your next barter deal.

fields.label: What exactly are you trading?
fields.model: 3 x 30–45 second videos per month, in exchange for a standing product supply.

fields.label: How will you disclose it?
fields.model: #gifted or #ad on every post, clearly and every time. This isn't optional in the UK or US.

fields.label: What can they do with your content?
fields.model: Brand can repost to their own social pages for 6 months. No paid ad usage without a new conversation.

fields.label: What happens if they ask for more later?
fields.model: Anything beyond the agreed videos per month is a new, paid ask, agreed in writing before you film it.

lessons.title: Turning Barter Work Into Paid Bookings
lessons.overview: A barter deal is a starting point, not a permanent arrangement. The whole reason it's worth doing is what it builds towards: real footage, a working relationship, and proof of what your content actually does for a brand. The skill is spotting the moment a free trade has earned the right to become a paid one.
lessons.interactive: Match each real barter outcome to the move it justifies.
lessons.deliverable: Write the exact message you'd send to turn one of your own barter deals into a paid booking.

activity.prompt: Match each situation to the right next move.
categories: Screenshot it and pitch a retainer
Ask for a rate card review

items.label: Your barter post for the café got 40k views and real comments asking where it is.
You've done 4 months of free trades with the same skincare brand, and they keep asking for more videos.
A brand you traded with wants to run your gifted video as a paid Meta ad.
You've done one trade with one brand and have no other proof yet.

wordbank.prompt: Drag each word into its blank. These pull from every module in the course.
wordbank.template: A great hook has to win the scroll in about three {0}. The direct-response structure every script follows is Hook, Agitate, Bridge, Offer, {1}. When a shadow looks harsh, {2} usually fixes it faster than moving the light. A retention graph shows you exactly where a viewer got {3} and left. Every UGC contract needs a {4} fee clause, or a cancelled job could pay you nothing. Views measure reach, but {5} and shares are what show a video actually connected. A brand running your video as a paid ad needs separate {6} terms, not just an organic repost. On a live shopping stream, the offer and urgency repeat the whole time instead of just {7}. Posting your own content regularly is proof of your style and consistency, which is why a real personal {8} tends to book more client work.

wheel.prompt: Spin to review. It skips topics you've already nailed and keeps retesting the ones you got wrong, so every spin makes real progress.

questions.q: Which studio tier did the course price at roughly £600 / $760?
questions.explain: Working Pro is the mid-tier, the point where gear stops being the bottleneck for most creators.

questions.q: In the 8-step production workflow, what should you confirm in writing before you even draft a script?
options: Usage rights, deadline, and revision count
questions.explain: Usage rights, deadline, and revision count. Getting this in writing before you draft anything is what prevents scope-creep and payment disputes later.

questions.q: How long does a viewer's scroll-stop decision actually take?
questions.explain: Under a second. That's why the first frame matters more than the first sentence.

questions.q: Which lever does a “POV: you just found out...” hook use?
questions.explain: Relatable POV. It puts the viewer directly inside a scenario they recognise, a different mechanism than a claim or a direct callout.

questions.q: What comes right after “Agitate” in the Hook, Agitate, Bridge, Offer, CTA structure?
questions.explain: Bridge is the pivot, it moves from the problem into your product as the solution.

questions.q: Which CTA type is built for a viewer who's already sold and just needs the next step?
questions.explain: Direct-Command. Once someone's convinced, telling them exactly what to do next removes friction instead of adding more convincing.

questions.q: What's the minimum number of angles the course says a single b-roll beat needs?
questions.explain: Three angles minimum, so an editor actually has something to cut between.

questions.q: What's the fix for a shot where the subject blends into an equally-bright background?
options: Add separation by dimming or moving the background light
questions.explain: Separation. Without a brightness gap between subject and background, the shot reads flat no matter the angle.

questions.q: What does a steep drop in the first 3 seconds of a retention graph usually mean?
questions.explain: A steep early drop almost always traces back to a weak or missing hook.

questions.q: What's the fastest way to clean up CapCut's auto-captions to broadcast quality?
options: Fix the wrong words, then apply keyword emphasis to the ones that matter
questions.explain: Auto-captions get you 90% there. Fixing the misheard words and adding keyword emphasis takes them the rest of the way, far faster than retyping.

questions.q: Which contract clause protects you if a client cancels the job halfway through?
questions.explain: A kill fee means a cancelled job still pays you something for the work already done.

questions.q: What's the fastest way to kill a cold pitch before it's even read?
options: A generic subject line and greeting
questions.explain: A generic subject line and greeting reads as a mass email, and most inboxes never make it past that first glance.

questions.q: A video has huge views but almost no comments, saves, or shares. What does that usually mean?
options: It got seen but didn't actually connect
questions.explain: Views alone measure reach, not resonance. Comments, saves, and shares are what show the content actually landed.

questions.q: For a direct-response client ad, which single metric matters most?
options: Total watch time across all videos
questions.explain: Direct-response is about action, not attention. Conversion ties straight back to what the client is actually paying for.

questions.q: A brand wants to run your video as a paid ad, not just repost it organically. What does that require?
options: Nothing extra, organic usage covers it
Just crediting you in the caption
questions.explain: Paid usage (ad-spend running behind your content) is a separate right from organic reposting, and it's priced separately.

questions.q: A contract says usage is “worldwide, all platforms, in perpetuity” with no extra pay for it. What is that?
options: A red flag, usage this broad should cost more or have a term limit
questions.explain: Unlimited usage forever is one of the broadest asks a brand can make. If it's not priced or time-limited, it's worth pushing back on.

questions.q: What's the main pacing difference between a scripted UGC video and a live shopping stream?
options: No difference, same structure works for both
Live selling repeats the offer and urgency continuously, not once at the end
Live streams should never mention price
questions.explain: A static video pitches once. A live stream has to keep re-hooking new viewers who join mid-stream, so the offer repeats constantly.

questions.q: How do most creators get paid for TikTok Shop / affiliate live selling?
options: A commission on what actually sells through their link or stream
Payment isn't possible on these platforms
questions.explain: Affiliate commission tied to actual sales is the core model, on top of any flat fee a brand may add for a dedicated live session.

questions.q: Why do creators who post their own content regularly tend to book more client work?
options: Brands can see real proof of their style and consistency, not just a reel
Personal content counts as free client work
questions.explain: A personal feed is proof you can produce content on your own, consistently. Brands read that as lower risk than a portfolio of one-off jobs.

questions.q: What's a content pillar?
options: A recurring topic or format you're known for, so your feed isn't random
questions.explain: Pillars are the 2-3 recurring themes that make an audience know what to expect from you, which turns random viewers into followers.

title: Book your 1:1
description: Book a 1:1 coaching call with ClickClick.

title: The CLocal Creator Playbook
description: Part Two of the Creator Track, less about the basics and more about how this actually turns into income: getting chosen by shops in the first place, what a 90-second clip is good for that isn't just "longer", judging whether a deal is genuinely worth your hours, and reading your own numbers so each shoot teaches you something for the next one. Coaching comes with it too, whenever you want to use it.

modules.title: Getting Chosen
modules.frame: Anyone can post a review. What actually gets you picked, again and again, by shops on the same street, is a different set of habits. This module is about being the creator a shop owner thinks of first.

lessons.title: Picking a Patch, Not Just a Shop
lessons.overview: One video for one shop is a fine start. Owning a street, an area, or a category is a different game, shop owners talk to each other, and the creator who's already reviewed three places on the same road tends to be the one who gets mentioned next. Worth thinking about which patch is actually yours.
lessons.interactive: A few questions worth sitting with about your own patch.
lessons.deliverable: If it's useful: sketch out 3 shops that make sense as your patch, and why.

activity.prompt: Questions worth sitting with when you're picking a patch.

items.text: Is there a street or area you're already in most weeks anyway?
Is there a category (coffee, food, fitness) you naturally notice more than others?
Would 3 shops on the same patch actually see each other's posts?
Is this somewhere you'd want to be known, not just post once and move on?

lessons.title: The Local Hook: Why “Best on This Street” Wins
lessons.overview: A generic hook is competing with the whole internet. A local hook is only up against the other three coffee shops on the same road, and the person watching already knows exactly where that road is. Naming the actual street or area is usually what makes a review feel like it's for the person watching it, not just anyone.
lessons.interactive: Have a go at a local hook for a few different shops, using this as a starting template.
lessons.deliverable: If you want to try it: write 3 local hooks, one for a different real or imagined shop each.

activity.prompt: A starting template for a local hook, for 3 different shops.

fields.label: Shop 1: [type of shop] on [street name]
fields.model: “The only proper flat white on Botanic Avenue.”

fields.label: Shop 2: [type of shop] on [street name]
fields.model: “If you live near the Cathedral Quarter, this is your new Sunday spot.”

fields.label: Shop 3: [type of shop] on [street name]
fields.model: “Three minutes from the train station and nobody's talking about it yet.”

lessons.title: 90 Seconds Is a Different Product, Not a Longer One
lessons.overview: It's tempting to think of 90 seconds as just more of a 45-second video. What it's actually good for is different: a cut a shop could put on their own page, not just yours. That's a genuinely different use, not a duration difference, and it's worth filming with that in mind from the start rather than padding out a shorter idea.
lessons.interactive: Match each extra beat a 90-second clip has room for to what it's actually doing.
lessons.deliverable: If you want to try it: reshoot one of your existing reviews at 90 seconds with the shop's own page in mind.

activity.prompt: Match each beat to what it's actually doing for a 90-second clip.
categories: Gives the shop something to repost

items.label: A few extra seconds on the owner or staff, not just the product
A wider shot that shows the actual room, not just a close-up
A clean closing line that works even with your voice cut out

lessons.title: Making Something the Shop Will Actually Repost
lessons.overview: Sending the shop owner a copy of the finished file, not just a link to your own page, is a small habit that changes a lot. A file they can actually repost, hand to staff, or save is a different thing to them than a link they'd have to remember to check.
lessons.interactive: A few habits worth building into how you hand work over.
lessons.deliverable: If it's useful: next time you finish a review, send the actual file, not just a link, and see if it changes anything.

activity.prompt: Habits worth building into how you hand a finished review over.

items.text: Send the actual video file, not just a link to your page
Mention they're welcome to repost it, so it's clearly not just yours
Turn it around within a few days, not a few weeks
Say thanks and name the next thing you'd like to film there, if there is one

modules.title: Turning It Into Income
modules.frame: The habits above get you chosen. This module is about what happens once you are: judging which deals are actually worth your time, approaching shops yourself, and reading your own numbers so each shoot teaches you something.

lessons.title: What Makes a Shop Ask You Back
lessons.overview: One good video gets you one shop. Getting asked back, tagged in their own posts, and recommended to other shop owners is almost never about the footage, it tends to come down to a few habits around it.
lessons.interactive: What's actually driving the shop owner's reaction in each of these moments?
lessons.deliverable: Worth a moment: which of these 3 habits are you weakest at, honestly, and one thing worth changing this week.

activity.prompt: What's actually driving the shop owner's reaction here?

questions.q: You said you'd film on Tuesday. You show up on Tuesday, on time, and it takes 15 minutes like you said it would. The owner seems almost surprised.
options: Basic reliability, doing what you said you'd do
questions.explain: Reliability. Most creators are vague about timing, so simply doing what you said is already memorable.

questions.q: You post the video 3 weeks later, after the owner's already asked about it twice.
options: A slow turnaround, even good footage, reads as unreliable
It doesn't matter as long as it's good
questions.explain: Turnaround matters as much as quality. A brilliant video that arrives 3 weeks late still teaches the owner not to rely on you.

questions.q: You never actually send the shop owner a copy of the finished file, just a link to your own page.
options: Fine, they can just watch it on your page
A missed chance, they can't repost or show it to staff without you
questions.explain: Send the file. It costs nothing and makes a shop owner feel like this was actually done for them.

lessons.title: Walking Into a Shop That Isn't on CLocal Yet
lessons.overview: Every shop on CLocal started as one that wasn't. Bringing one on yourself is one of the more reliable ways to guarantee you've always got somewhere to film, and it's a real, useful pitch once you've got a way to say it.
lessons.interactive: Two creators approach the same local shop about being on CLocal. Read both, then see which one you'd bet on.
lessons.deliverable: If it's useful: approach a few local shops that aren't on CLocal yet, and keep a note of each one for yourself.

dmMockup.bad: hey do you want to be on my tiktok
dmMockup.good: Hi! I'm a CLocal creator, I review local spots on the app and I'd love to feature you. It's a quick 90-second video, no cost to you, and it puts you in front of people nearby who're already looking for exactly this. Would this week work?

activity.prompt: Read both approaches to the same local shop, then answer.

questions.q:
Pitch A: “hey do you want to be on my tiktok”
Pitch B: “Hi! I'm a CLocal creator, I review local spots on the app and I'd love to feature you. It's a quick 90-second video, no cost to you, and it puts you in front of people nearby who're already looking for exactly this. Would this week work?”
Which one would you bet gets a reply?
questions.explain: Pitch B tends to do better. It names the actual app, the actual format, the actual cost (none), and asks a specific question the owner can say yes to quickly.

questions.q: What's the one thing Pitch B does that makes it easy to say yes to fast?
options: It suggests an exact, low-effort format and asks about a specific timeframe
questions.explain: Specifics. “This week” and “90-second video, no cost” turn a vague favour into a small, concrete yes.

lessons.title: Judging Whether a Deal Is Worth Your Hours
lessons.overview: Not every gift deal is worth claiming, and that's fine, it's your call either way. Worth weighing up roughly what the product's actually worth against how long it'll realistically take you, and knowing it's fine to ask for a bit more before you commit, or just pass.
lessons.interactive: Would you take these deals, pass, or ask for more first? Have a think, then see how others tend to call it.
lessons.deliverable: If it's useful: next time you're offered a deal, actually weigh product value against your hours before deciding.

activity.prompt: Take it, pass, or ask for more first?

questions.q: A café offers a £6 pastry bundle for one video that'll take you about 20 minutes, somewhere you already go anyway.
questions.explain: Reasonable value for the time, and you're there anyway. A solid, low-effort yes.

questions.q: A homeware shop offers one candle (roughly £8) for 3 videos and exclusive rights for 6 months.
questions.explain: Worth asking first. The ask (3 videos, 6-month exclusivity) is a lot for one candle, a quick message asking for more product or fewer videos costs you nothing.

questions.q: A new gym offers a free week's pass for one video, no exclusivity, no extra terms.
questions.explain: Clear terms, reasonable trade, no catch. Worth taking if it's a place you'd genuinely visit.

lessons.title: Reading Your Own Numbers
lessons.overview: Creator Studio shows your total views and how many videos you've posted, worth checking every so often rather than never. The point isn't to obsess over one number, it's noticing which clips actually got watched and what they had in common, so the next shoot isn't a total guess. Worth getting your payout details saved too, so there's nothing to chase later once money's moving.
lessons.interactive: A few questions worth asking next time you check your numbers.
lessons.deliverable: If it's useful: pick your best-performing review so far and write a sentence on what you think made it work.

activity.prompt: Worth asking yourself next time you check your numbers.

items.text: Which review has the most views so far, and what's different about it?
Is there a shop type or hook style showing up more than once in your best clips?
Are your payout details actually saved, so nothing's held up later?
Is there one thing worth trying differently on your next shoot?

title: The CLocal Creator Field Guide
description: You're approved and you're posting, that's the part most people never get past. This walks through how CLocal actually works, what you can do in your first half hour, and the things that decide whether a review lands: a 45-second shape worth trying, filming in a real shop, and claiming your first gift deal. Nothing here is the only way to do it, just a place to start. Part One of the Creator Track.

modules.title: How CLocal Works
modules.frame: Before any filming technique, it helps to actually see how the app fits together, and to do a few low-stakes things inside it so it stops feeling brand new. Nothing in this module involves a shop or a camera.

lessons.title: What CLocal Actually Is
lessons.overview: It's a loop, not a list of features. People nearby open CLocal to find somewhere to go. Your review sits on the feed and the map next to a real shop. Shops on CLocal put up gift deals and pay for visibility. Your referral code brings in members. Each part feeds the next one.
lessons.interactive: See if you can guess the order this loop actually runs in, there's no wrong way to start.
lessons.deliverable: If it helps, sketch this loop out somewhere you'll see it again, in your own words.

activity.prompt: Have a go at ordering how this loop actually connects, then see how close you were.
items: Someone nearby opens CLocal looking for somewhere to go
Your review shows up on the feed and the map next to a real shop
Shops on CLocal post gift deals and pay for visibility
Your referral code brings in new members

lessons.title: The Four Ways Something Comes Back to You
lessons.overview: There's more than one way this pays off, and they land on different timelines. A gift deal can land the same day. Your referral code adds up week by week, and it's recurring, not a one-off, for as long as that person stays a member. A shop asking you back happens over weeks. Your profile becoming real leverage takes months. None of these need the others to be worth doing.
lessons.interactive: See what a few different referral counts could actually add up to.
lessons.deliverable: Worth a look: work out roughly what your own numbers might be, whenever you've got a few referrals to plug in.

activity.prompt: See what a few real referral counts could look like over a month.

fields.label: VIP referrals through your code this month

activity.modelNote: Commission payouts are being switched on soon, so treat this as the model to understand now, not cash landing immediately. It's recurring though, not a one-off: every referral keeps paying out monthly for as long as they stay a member, and it stacks as you add more. Build up to 200 active referrals over time (roughly 4 a week for a year) and that's about £599 landing every month, on repeat.

lessons.title: Your First Half Hour in the App
lessons.overview: Before you go anywhere near a shop, there's a handful of things worth doing inside the app itself, none of them need a camera. Getting these done first tends to make everything after feel less like starting from nothing.
lessons.interactive: A few small things worth doing in the app before your first shoot.
lessons.deliverable: If it helps: work through these at your own pace, in whatever order suits you.

activity.prompt: Nothing here needs a shop or a camera, just a few minutes in the app.

items.text: Add a real photo and a one-line description to your profile
Find your referral link and save it somewhere you can grab it fast
Browse the open gift deals and shortlist a few you'd genuinely claim
Save a few shops near you that you'd like to review

modules.title: Your First Reviews
modules.frame: The craft side: a shape for a 45-second review worth trying, a few things worth checking before you film in someone else's shop, and what claiming a gift deal actually involves.

lessons.title: What 45 Seconds Actually Needs
lessons.overview: 45 seconds isn't much room for a slow build. One shape that tends to work: a hook, the thing itself, and a verdict, nothing more. It's one option, not the only one, but it's a solid place to start if you're not sure.
lessons.interactive: One order that tends to work for a 45-second review, have a go at putting it together.
lessons.deliverable: If you want to try it: post one and paste the link, just for your own reference.

Give your honest one-line verdict and close

lessons.title: Filming Inside a Real Shop Without Feeling Awkward
lessons.overview: It's a real shop with real customers, not a studio, and there's no retake budget. A few things other creators say they wish they'd checked before their first few shoots.
lessons.interactive: Things creators say they wish they'd checked before filming in a shop.
lessons.deliverable: Worth noticing: which of these you'd have skipped before this lesson, and why it matters now.

activity.prompt: Things creators say they wish they'd checked before filming in a shop.

items.text: Told the owner or staff what you're filming
Checked nobody's face is in frame without them knowing
Filmed towards the light rather than with it behind you, if it's dark
Picked a quieter moment for the one line you need clean audio on
Knew your one shot before starting, rather than figuring it out mid-take

lessons.title: Claiming Your First Gift Deal
lessons.overview: Claiming a gift is a small agreement, worth understanding properly. Whatever the offer said the moment you claimed it is what it stays, even if the shop changes it afterwards, and even if you get busy. Getting this right is what keeps gift deals open to creators generally.
lessons.interactive: What have you actually agreed to in each of these gift-claim moments?
lessons.deliverable: If you're ready: claim one real gift deal, and keep a note of which shop it was with.

activity.prompt: What have you actually agreed to?

questions.q: You claim a gift offer from a bakery. What have you actually agreed to?
options: Nothing until you feel like it
One review video, on the terms shown at the moment you claimed it
As many videos as they end up wanting
questions.explain: One video, on the terms locked in when you claimed. That's the whole deal, no more and no less.

questions.q: A week after you claim, the bakery changes their public offer to ask for 2 videos instead of 1. Do you now owe 2?
options: Yes, always match the latest version
No, your terms were locked in the moment you claimed
questions.explain: No. Your terms are locked in at claim time. What they post afterwards doesn't change what you already agreed to.

questions.q: You claimed a gift, got busy, and never filmed anything. What's the actual cost?
options: Nothing really, it's only a coffee
The shop loses trust in CLocal creators generally, and you may lose access to future gifts
questions.explain: It's bigger than one coffee. Unfulfilled claims are the fastest way for a shop, and CLocal, to stop trusting creators with gifts.

lessons.title: You've Done One Shop, What's Next?
lessons.overview: Once you've posted a review and claimed a deal, a natural question shows up: how do you stop doing this one shop at a time? That's really what Part Two of the Creator Track is about, longer clips, a different way of getting chosen by shops, and turning gift deals into repeat, paid work. No rush either way, it's there whenever it's useful.
lessons.interactive: A short reflection on how your first shop actually went.
lessons.deliverable: Worth a moment: write 2–3 sentences on what surprised you most about your first shop.

activity.prompt: A few things worth checking in on now that you've done one shop.

items.text: Posted at least one review you're happy with
Claimed or shortlisted a gift deal
Shared your referral link somewhere real
Have a rough idea which shop you'd want to film again
